1:
A boy of eight comes to the throne, and the witnesses weigh when he began in earnest. Most read the eighth year as the eighth of the reign, making him sixteen when he began to seek the God of David — Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical), Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical), Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) and John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) all agree, Wesley adding that it was just as he entered the age of temptation, the government in his own hands and none to restrain him. John Gill (reformed) agrees but preserves two other readings: Kimchi takes it for the year he began to reign, the eighth of his age, while Jarchi renders the clause as a concession, that though he was young he began to seek God. Henry presses that Josiah had nothing like Manasseh's education and may have had those about him who wished to corrupt him, yet sought God early — the duty and honour of the young, since those who seek him early shall find him.

The chronology of the purge is the real crux, since Chronicles dates it to the twelfth year and Kings to the eighteenth. Henry supposes something was done at twelve, that the work met opposition and was not thorough until the book of the law was found six years later, and that the historian has laid the whole together briefly. Ellicott argues the same from the text, noting that the closing verse implies the work was unfinished at twelve, and that a writer who has begun the story naturally carries it to its close. He then reports and rejects two modern explanations: that the chronicler put the extirpation first to show the king needed no prompting, which Thenius asserts, and that he meant to clear so praised a king of tolerating the abomination for eighteen years, which Noldeke supposes. Keil and Delitzsch call the Chronicle the more exact of the two, since Kings views the whole reform in connection with the finding of the book while the Chronicle keeps the events apart and in their order of time.

On the encomium they converge, and Ellicott supplies the fact that gives it weight: Josiah is the only king of whom it is said he declined neither to the right hand nor to the left, which amounts to saying his observance of the law was perfect. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) reads it as a double guard, timidity not keeping him from going far enough nor zeal carrying him beyond due bounds, so that he walked in the golden mean; Henry puts it that there are errors on both hands.

The demolition draws close notes. Gill has the king present in person, not merely issuing orders, and notes that these were Manasseh's altars, cast out at his humiliation and rebuilt by his son. Ellicott confirms from Kings that Josiah superintended the work himself, renders the images as sun statues, and remarks on the strange turn by which the dust was sprinkled on the graves of those who had sacrificed, as if the graves were guilty. Keil and Delitzsch explain the burning of the priests' bones on their altars as a deliberate defilement of the place with the ashes of the dead, Ellicott noting the horror with which such violation was then regarded. Gill accounts for Josiah's authority in the northern cities by the Assyrian captivity having left the remnant subject to Judah, while Keil and Delitzsch explain why Simeon is counted among the northern tribes — geographically it belonged to Judah, but in religion it stayed attached to the high places. They also find the phrase describing that northern progress unintelligible as it stands, canvassing a rabbinic rendering of mountain-dwellings which the words cannot bear, the Greek which gives simply their places, the Targum which has the house of their desolation, and the marginal reading with their swords.
8:
The repair begins in the eighteenth year, and John Gill (reformed) reckons the king then twenty-six, with six years of purging behind him. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks the order as the pattern: having cleansed the house he now fits it for its services, as the heart must be cleansed before it is renewed into God's image; and he notices that Josiah calls God the Lord his God, since those who love God will love the habitation of his house. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes a difference of form rather than substance, that Kings gives this material as the king's instructions to Shaphan while the Chronicle reports them carried out.

On one phrase all three of the close readers desert the English. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) holds that for and they returned we should read the inhabitants, a reading supported by many manuscripts and printed editions and all the versions, as well as by necessity and common sense. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) say the same from the other end, that the marginal reading is a correction arising from a misunderstanding of the written text, which gives the dwellers in Jerusalem. Ellicott states it briefly: the margin yields the familiar rendering, but the Hebrew text has the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and is correct. On the contributors, Keil and Delitzsch judge the enumeration from the hand of Manasseh and Ephraim rhetorical, and Ellicott rejects Reuss's attempt to make it an organised collection throughout the land and draw from that an inference unfavourable to the chronicler.

The craftsmen are praised, and Henry takes the praise seriously: workmen are not completely faithful unless both careful and diligent, since a confidence is reposed in them. Ellicott gives the literal sense, that the men were dealing in good faith, and recalls that in Kings this is the ground on which the high priest is told to require no account of the money. Gill has the burden-bearers overseen lest they be dilatory or the workmen stand idle for want of materials. On what was being mended, Ellicott renders the flooring as raftering and the houses as the chambers — John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) agrees they are the chambers adjoining the temple — and he alone softens the charge against the earlier kings, suggesting that destroyed may mean no more than allowed to go to ruin.

Why the overseers were chosen from Levites skilled in music divides them four ways, and it is the chapter's liveliest question. Clarke asks outright whether the musicians played to enliven the workmen, and argues it from a discovery then newly made: a Greek treatise on music recovered from the cities buried beneath Vesuvius shows the harper of the Theban legend was employed by the workmen to play while they laboured, and paid from their wages, so that the walls the fable says rose to his music rose because his music lightened the toil. Ellicott thinks they probably did cheer the labour with song, as in ancient Egypt, and observes that the term for setting the work forward is usually a musical one, so the honourable standing of the musical guilds is worth noticing. Wesley supposes instead that they were exercised in both employments by turns, overseeing the work and praising God with voice and instrument. Henry denies the connection: their skill in music could be of no use in architecture, and is mentioned only as evidence that they were men of sense whose genius lay toward the mathematics, which qualified them for the trust — witty men being wise men when they employ their wit in doing good. He draws his own lesson from the pairing: God dispenses his gifts variously, some cut out for bodily labour and some for oversight, the one the hands and the other the heads, each needing the other and bound to serve the other in love.
14:
The book turns up while the money is brought out, and where exactly is disputed. Keil and Delitzsch (grammatical-historical) are careful to say that the words do not clearly imply he found it where the money was laid up. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that this verse is absent from Kings and supplements the older account by supplying the occasion, then reports two traditions: Josephus has the high priest find it in the treasure-chamber, which he had entered to fetch gold and silver for making sacred vessels, while rabbinic tradition has it hidden under a heap of stones to save it from being burnt by Ahaz. John Gill (reformed) traces only the chain of hands, the Levites bringing the money from the country to the temple, the high priest passing it to the king's ministers and they to the overseers, so the repairs began.

What the book was, both close readers agree, is not Moses' own copy. Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase about Moses characterises it as the book of the Mosaic law and not necessarily as his autograph; Ellicott reaches the same by syntax, holding that the phrase by the hand of Moses attaches not to the book but to the law of Jehovah, so that the sense is the law communicated through Moses' instrumentality. Ellicott also corrects the English article: the Hebrew gives the book, not a book. He twice refuses to let the wording carry inferences about its size: when Kings adds that Shaphan read it, those words need not mean he read it through, as Thenius suggests, and the chronicler's read in it may mean the same thing, so it is too much to suppose he altered the phrase to insinuate the book was bulky.

The king's reaction is where Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) puts the weight. He begins from what the scene should make a later reader feel — that Bibles are jewels but, thanks be to God, not rarities, the fountain no longer a spring shut up but a stream flowing for common use — and warns that we shall have much to answer for if the great things of God's law, being made common, come to be accounted strange. On the rent clothes he notes that God was pleased with the gesture, yet turns it inward: were these things as new to us as to Josiah they would cut deeper, and they are not less weighty for being well known, so rend the heart and not the garments. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) makes the same point in nearly the same words. Henry adds that the chapter directs us, under conviction of sin, to enquire of the Lord as Josiah did, having the lively oracles to bring such enquiries to.

The oracle's wording draws Ellicott's sharpest redactional judgement. Where the king asks for those left in Israel and Judah, he notes the alteration from the simpler phrase in Kings and infers the chronicler is thinking of the northern remnant; and where this text says the wrath is poured out while Kings and the Greek have it kindled against, he argues that Kings is probably original, since the wrath Josiah dreaded had not yet been poured out upon Judah — but the chronicler remembered the ruin of the ten tribes. He finds the list of messengers defective in the Hebrew and would restore it from the Greek, or better from the Syriac and Latin, noting a plausible correction in three manuscripts; he settles the variant spellings in Huldah's genealogy by weighing the versions; and he renders the place she lived not a college but the second quarter, that is the lower city. Keil and Delitzsch treat the small differences here as clarifications rather than discrepancies, holding that the chronicler's way of putting the delivery of the book makes the matter plainer without altering the facts.
24:
The threat the prophetess returns is drawn from the law the king has just heard read. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) notes that the opening is a participle, so that God is about to bring the evil rather than merely resolved on it, and that the phrase about all the curses written in the book is the chronicler's explanatory paraphrase of the simpler words of Kings — the curses in view being those of Deuteronomy, which he lists. Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) draws the general warning, that those who forsake God bring evil on themselves and kindle a fire which shall not be quenched, as the fire of his wrath will be when the decree has gone out against the impenitent.

Ellicott finds the chronicler's own hand visible throughout the oracle, and consistently in one direction. Where this text says the wrath is poured out, Kings has it kindled, which he judges the better reading since it agrees with the promise that it shall not be quenched; the clause about the king humbling himself before God is absent from Kings and is, he says, a characteristic repetition; the words added about the inhabitants of the place are the chronicler's; the grave is a plural in the Hebrew; and small adjustments of verb form and emphasis run through the whole. Taken together these show a writer pressing the theme of humbling, which is the very thing the oracle turns on.

Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) stops at the clause about the tender heart, and for a reason that has nothing to do with collation. He renders the Targum's version — that the king's heart was melted and he humbled himself in the sight of the Word of the Lord when he heard his words against this place — and points out that the paraphrast there uses two different terms, one for the Word as a person and another for a word merely spoken or expressed. The distinction, he holds, is unmistakable in the Targum itself.

The promise that closes the oracle is what Henry dwells on. Josiah's humbling will not turn the wrath from the land, yet it delivers his own soul; and good people are taught by it to be so far from fearing death as to welcome it when it takes them away from the evil to come. He observes how the whole property of the thing is altered by being made the matter of a promise — gathered to the grave in peace, housed in that ark as Noah was when a deluge was coming. Clarke refers the reader to his fuller treatment of the same promise elsewhere.
29:
The king gathers everyone and reads the book himself, and Matthew Henry (puritan-evangelical) marks the order of it: he did not force them to their duty until he had instructed them in it, calling great and small, young and old, rich and poor, since all were concerned in the words. That the king read rather than the priests put honour on the service, and Henry supposes he read so as to show he was himself affected, which would affect his hearers. John Gill (reformed) notes only that from here to the end the account runs as it does in Kings. Charles Ellicott (grammatical-historical) finds one substitution worth explaining: where Kings has the prophets among the assembly this text has the Levites, a natural change for a writer in whose day the prophetic order was long extinct, though he allows it may be an unconscious slip, the phrase about priests and Levites being so frequent in his pages. On the king's standing he glosses the Hebrew as on his stand, and takes the word Kings uses for the dais to be synonymous.

What the people then did divides them. Adam Clarke (wesleyan-arminian) takes it physically: the king likely made them all rise as the terms were read, so testifying their approbation of the covenant and their resolve to keep it faithfully and perseveringly. John Wesley (wesleyan-arminian) takes it as a binding act, that he made them engage by oath or covenant to observe the laws of God as his predecessors had done and as they were already obliged to do. Henry has both king and people subscribe the articles, the king covenanting in his place to keep the commandments with all his heart, and then urging the people to declare their consent. Ellicott suspects the verse was disturbed in transmission: Kings and the Syriac both say the people came into the covenant, and since the verbs for standing and causing to stand differ only in vowels anciently unwritten, he judges the phrase about Benjamin a likely corruption of the words about entering the covenant, which the sense requires here as much as there. He notes too that the closing remark about the inhabitants keeping the covenant has no counterpart in Kings.

On whether any of it held, Henry and Ellicott arrive independently at the same verdict and cite the same prophet. Ellicott allows that the royal will secured an outward conformity, open idolatry being for the time too dangerous to attempt, but calls the unreality of reformations by royal mandate proved by the relapse that followed immediately on Josiah's death, and points to the pages of Jeremiah for the moral corruption then preying on the nation's vitals. Henry says the same from the other side: all Josiah's days were days of restraint upon a people with a bent to backslide, many wanting nothing but to have him out of the way; Jeremiah charged Judah with returning feignedly rather than with her whole heart, and the iniquity that ruined the house of Judah is dated from the very year of the reformation. Henry's conclusion is the sharpest thing in the chapter — that nothing hastens the ruin of a people, or ripens them for it, more than the baffling of hopeful attempts at reformation and a hypocritical return to God.

Both Henry and Wesley end on the doubled verb: that he made them serve, even serve, shows this was the one thing his heart was set upon, and that he aimed at nothing else but to engage them to God and their duty. Gill takes the clearing of the abominations to cover all the idols already related, and Ellicott observes that the sweep through the ten tribes' territories glances back to the earlier notice and summarises in one line what Kings sets out at length.
